analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act while keeping its Indian health care provisions.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a single cosponsor and never came up for a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act and its companion reconciliation law 60 days after passage, then restore the older health care rules that the 2010 law replaced. It carves out one exception: it keeps the reauthorization of the Indian Health Care Improvement Act, which funds health services for Native Americans. The bill was referred to seven committees, then to two health subcommittees, and went no further.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the biggest winners would have been high-income households, because the health provisions of the 2010 reconciliation law included the extra Medicare taxes on high earners and investment income that helped pay for coverage expansions. Health insurance companies would have been freed from the law's requirements, including rules on how much premium revenue they must spend on medical care rather than overhead and profit, and brand-name drug makers and medical device makers would have avoided fees and price concessions in the law. At the same time, tens of millions of people would have lost protections and coverage, so the gains to industry and the wealthy would have come at a direct cost to patients.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, insurers, drug and device makers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would repeal the Medicare surtaxes on high earners and investment income included in title I of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, cutting taxes for the highest-income households.

Repeal would remove the Affordable Care Act's insurance regulations, including the requirement that insurers spend a set share of premiums on medical care, along with its subsidies that brought customers into the insurance market.
It would eliminate the fees and price concessions the law imposed on brand-name drug makers and medical device makers.
It preserves the reauthorization of the Indian Health Care Improvement Act, funding health services for Native Americans.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, ordinary people who gained coverage or protections under the 2010 law would bear the cost: the law let young adults stay on a parent's plan, barred insurers from denying coverage or charging more for pre-existing conditions, expanded Medicaid, and provided tax credits that made private coverage affordable. Repeal would have taken those away and restored the pre-2010 system. Seniors would pay more for prescription drugs under Medicare, and people with pre-existing conditions would face the individual market as it existed before the law.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and low-income families

drawbacks.text: Repeal would have ended protections for people with pre-existing conditions, the requirement that young adults be allowed to stay on a parent's insurance, and the tax credits that made coverage affordable for lower- and middle-income families.

Repeal would have eliminated the Medicaid expansion and the subsidies that the Congressional Budget Office estimated would extend coverage to millions of uninsured Americans, restoring the pre-2010 system in which tens of millions went without insurance.

The bill was never developed: it attracted no cosponsors, was referred to seven committees without a provision-level breakdown, and never received a hearing or a vote, so there was no realistic plan for replacing the coverage it would have taken away.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs of repeal to ordinary people — losing pre-existing condition protections, dependent coverage, subsidies, and the Medicaid expansion — far outweigh the tax relief it would have handed to high earners and the deregulation it would have handed to insurers and drug makers. The one clear public benefit it contained, continuing Indian Health Care Improvement Act funding, was a carve-out the bill's author preserved while repealing the rest. The bill also failed on its own terms: it was a statement bill with no cosponsors and no path to passage, so its repeal provisions were never seriously negotiated.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee — bounced among seven of them and then two health subcommittees — and died there without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on January 7, 2011, with no cosponsors.
The Speaker's office referred it to seven committees: Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means, House Administration, Rules, Judiciary, and Appropriations.

In February 2011 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Education and Workforce Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee, and no further action followed for the rest of the Congress.
The bill never received a hearing or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the people it would have affected kept the 2010 law's protections: coverage for pre-existing conditions, dependent coverage for young adults, the Medicaid expansion, and the subsidies that helped low- and middle-income families buy insurance. High earners kept paying the Medicare surtaxes that had been created to finance those benefits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyone covered by the 2010 health law

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act while preserving the Indian Health Care Improvement Act reauthorization.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so no party-line split appears in the record; it was a one-member bill in a chamber whose majority did not act on it.

industries.note: Repeal would have freed insurers from the Affordable Care Act's rules, including the requirement to spend a set share of premiums on patient care, but would also have ended the subsidies that brought them millions of subsidized customers. The net effect is that insurers would have shed obligations that protect consumers.

Title I of the 2010 reconciliation law imposed extra Medicare taxes on high earners and investment income to fund coverage expansions; repeal would have removed them, shifting the cost of repeal onto everyone who would have lost coverage.
The 2010 law required drug makers to provide discounts on Medicare prescription drugs; repeal would have ended that concession, raising drug costs for seniors.
Repeal would have eliminated the tax the law placed on medical devices, at the cost of funding for the coverage expansions it helped pay for.

industries.industry: Hospitals and providers serving low-income patients
industries.note: Providers had accepted lower Medicare and Medicaid payment increases in exchange for millions of newly insured patients; repeal would have restored the payment cuts while taking away the coverage, leaving them with fewer paying patients. Indian Health Service funding, the one piece this bill preserved, supports a distinct network of Native health programs.
